newsitem.title: USA: U.S. suspends proposed Japan shipping sanctions.
newsitem.headline: U.S. suspends proposed Japan shipping sanctions.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) said on Tuesday that it has suspended proposed sanctions against Japanese shipping companies until September 4.

The decision came after John Graykowski, deputy administrator of the U.S. Maritime Administration, visited Tokyo on Monday to assess progress in the the reform of port practices there that were agreed upon by the U.S. and Japanese governments in April, the commission said in a news release.

The FMC proposed sanctions on November 6, 1996, against Japanese liner operators in response to restrictions on the use of Japanese ports. Those proposed sanctions included a $100,000 surcharge on Japanese shipping companies each time their vessels entered a U.S. port from abroad.

The suspension of sanctions will give Japan more time to resolve the port problems. Graykowski told Japanese government and shipping officials that he was concerned about "very little visible progress" since the April agreement, the statement said.

Graykowski, who was traveling with representatives of the U.S. departments of Transportation, State and Commerce, focused on the slow pace of reform in the so-called "prior consultation" system, which requires Japanese and foreign ocean carriers to obtain advance approval from the Japan Harbor Transportation Association (JHTA) for proposed changes in port operations.

"Among other things, the agreement reached by the two governments established a specific framework for significantly reforming this costly, arbitrary and non-transparent system by July 31, 1997," the statement said. "Mr. Graykowski stressed the need for tangible results as enumerated in the (April agreement)."
